describe the nature of alpha (α) particles, beta (β−) particles and gamma (γ) rays, and recall that they may be distinguished in terms of penetrating power and ability to ionise

primer.text: Unstable nuclei shed their excess energy by emitting ionising radiation: alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays. This note explains why decay happens, what each emission is made of, and how penetration and ionising power set the three apart.

lessons.title: Unstable nuclei and radioactive decay
lessons.opening: A nucleus is radioactive when a proton-neutron imbalance makes it unstable, and it decays by emitting radiation — a high-energy particle or wave — to reach a more stable state. The emissions are alpha, beta and gamma, and the timing of any single decay is random.
keyPoints: Unstable nuclei have an imbalance of protons or neutrons.
Radioactive decay is the emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus to gain stability.
The emitted radiations are alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Decay events are spontaneous and random — a single nucleus cannot be timed.
Carbon-14 carries two neutrons more than carbon-12, and that imbalance leaves it unstable.

low.restatement: An overloaded nucleus throws out a particle or a burst of energy. That loss leaves it more settled, like letting steam off a pressurised pot.
low.analogy: Radioactive decay is a wobbly stack of blocks toppling a few blocks off — the remaining stack stands steadier.
low.examPointer: The words "random" and "spontaneous" are mark-carrying: no cause, no clock, no prediction for one nucleus.

medium.restatement: Decay releases energy because the daughter arrangement has lower energy than the parent; the emitted particle or photon carries the difference away. Randomness means each nucleus has a constant decay probability per unit time, independent of its history.
medium.analogy: Each unstable nucleus is a lottery ticket with the same tiny winning chance every second — winning (decaying) is unpredictable for any single ticket even though the odds never change.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish radiation (the emission) from radioactivity (the property of the nucleus); questions probe the vocabulary.

check.stem: Which statement about radioactive decay is true?

options.text: the timing of a single nucleus’s decay cannot be predicted
options.explanation: Decay is a random process — no prediction is possible for one nucleus.

options.text: scientists can predict when each nucleus will decay
options.explanation: Randomness forbids per-nucleus prediction.

options.text: decay happens only in artificial sources
options.explanation: Unstable nuclei decay wherever they are, natural or not.

options.text: decay always emits all three radiations at once
options.explanation: A given decay emits one type (or a subset), not necessarily all three.

check.stem: What causes a nucleus to be unstable?

options.text: an imbalance of protons or neutrons
options.explanation: The proton-neutron balance is what the nucleus is sensitive to.
Electrons do not destabilise the nucleus.
Nuclear stability is unrelated to the atomic radius.
Decay needs no external light — it is spontaneous.

check.stem: Why is carbon-14 unstable while carbon-12 is stable?

options.explanation: The two additional neutrons unbalance the nucleus.
Both carbon isotopes have 6 protons.
Stability is not about ionisation.
Electron count is irrelevant to nuclear stability.

check.stem: What happens to a nucleus when it emits radiation?

options.explanation: The emission carries energy away, settling the nucleus.
Decay is the route towards stability.
The nucleus remains, transformed.
Emission, not absorption, defines decay.

check.stem: Radiation from a decaying nucleus can be…

options.text: a high-energy particle or a high-energy wave
options.explanation: Alpha and beta are particles; gamma is a wave of the electromagnetic kind.
Gamma rays are waves, not particles.
Alpha and beta are particles.
The emissions are subatomic, not whole atoms.

check.stem: Name the three types of radiation emitted from unstable nuclei.
check.modelAnswer: The three emissions are alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Radioactive decay is the process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation — a particle or wave — and becomes more stable.

check.stem: Explain why it is impossible to state the moment when one particular unstable nucleus will decay.
check.modelAnswer: Radioactive decay is a random process: each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in any interval, but nothing about its history or surroundings marks the exact moment.

check.stem: A student claims carbon-14 should be stable because it is carbon. Use the proton-neutron story to correct them.
check.modelAnswer: Being carbon fixes 6 protons but not stability; carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, two more than the stable carbon-12, and that proton-neutron imbalance makes its nucleus unstable.

lessons.title: Alpha, beta and gamma: nature and penetration
sourceHeadings: Penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma
lessons.opening: The three radiations differ in what they are and how far they travel. Alpha is a helium nucleus stopped by paper, beta is a fast electron stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is an electromagnetic wave only reduced by thick lead — with ionising power falling in the reverse order.
keyPoints: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
A beta particle is a high-energy electron created when a neutron becomes a proton.
Gamma rays are the highest-energy electromagnetic waves, with no mass or charge.
Alpha is the least penetrating and the most ionising; gamma is the most penetrating and the least ionising.
Paper stops alpha; a few millimetres of aluminium stop beta; only several centimetres of lead reduce gamma.

low.restatement: Line up three barriers — paper, thin aluminium, thick lead. Alpha dies at the paper, beta dies at the aluminium, gamma ploughs on until lead slows it.
low.analogy: Alpha is a bowling ball (huge impact, barely travels), beta a thrown pebble, gamma a laser beam that goes far but nudges lightly.
low.examPointer: Pair the properties in reverse: most ionising = least penetrating. Questions love that inversion.

medium.restatement: Ionising ability tracks charge and size: the heavy, double-charged alpha rips electrons from atoms most effectively but collides and stops soonest; the massless gamma interacts rarely, so it penetrates furthest while ionising least. Absorber choice follows directly.
medium.analogy: A heavy truck stops at the first wall but wrecks it; a bullet goes further with less smash; a searchlight passes over everything while barely touching it.
medium.examPointer: Absorption tables are free marks if you attach each radiation to its absorber — and remember the beta/aluminium thickness nuance.

check.stem: What is an alpha particle identical to?

options.explanation: Alpha = 2 protons + 2 neutrons, the helium nucleus.
Hydrogen has one proton — not the alpha composition.
That is a beta particle.
That is gamma radiation.
Beta is stopped by several millimetres of aluminium.
Paper stops alpha; beta sails through.

options.text: a few centimetres of air only
options.explanation: Beta travels tens of centimetres in air.
Aluminium stops beta readily.

check.stem: Which radiation has the greatest ionising power?

options.explanation: Alpha is the most strongly ionising of the three.
Beta ionises moderately.
Gamma is the weakest ioniser.
The three differ sharply in ionising ability.

check.stem: Gamma rays are best described as…

options.explanation: Gamma is wave radiation with no mass or charge.
That is alpha.
Neutron emission is a separate, rarer decay mode.
Beta electrons are fast, and gamma is not an electron at all.

check.stem: A source’s count rate falls sharply behind 5 mm of aluminium but barely changes behind paper or 5 mm of lead. Which radiation is emitted?

options.explanation: Aluminium absorption identifies beta; paper and lead transparency exclude alpha and significant gamma.
Alpha would have been stopped by the paper.
Gamma would pass aluminium and be cut by thick lead.
The paper result already rules alpha out.

check.stem: State what a beta particle is and how it is produced inside a nucleus.
check.modelAnswer: A beta particle is a high-energy electron, produced when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron.

check.stem: Give the absorber that stops each of alpha, beta and gamma.
check.modelAnswer: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by several centimetres of lead.

check.stem: Explain why gamma is the most penetrating of the three radiations even though it is the weakest ioniser.
check.modelAnswer: Gamma photons carry no charge and no mass, so they interact with matter only rarely; each interaction loses little energy, letting gamma travel far, while its weak interaction is also why it ionises least.

check.stem: Count rates behind absorbers are: bare 4320, paper 4318, 5 mm aluminium 256, 5 mm lead 244. Identify the radiation and justify each step.
check.modelAnswer: Paper barely changes the count (4320 → 4318), so no alpha; aluminium cuts it sharply (4320 → 256), so beta is present; lead leaves a similar residual (244), so no significant gamma. The source emits beta.

glossary.definition: The random emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus, leaving it more stable.
A helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) emitted from an unstable nucleus.
A high-energy electron emitted when a nucleus converts a neutron into a proton.
A high-energy electromagnetic wave emitted from a nucleus, with no mass or charge.
